Computer-aided Lyapunov analyses in optimization

October 23, 2026

Many con­ver­gence proofs for first-order meth­ods in op­ti­mi­za­tion follow a common pattern: construct a Lyapunov function, establish an inequality describing its decrease, and use this inequality to show that a performance measure converges to zero. Within many standard problem classes and prescribed families of Lyapunov functions, these tasks can often be formulated exactly as semi­definite programs (SDPs). Existing solvers can then be used to search numerically for feasible solutions. Con­ver­gence analysis itself thus becomes a tractable op­ti­mi­za­tion problem.

Closely related is the performance estimation problem (PEP) methodology, introduced by Drori and Teboulle [DT14]. For many first-order meth­ods and problem classes, the search for a worst-case example can be reformulated as an SDP, giving tight worst-case guarantees [THG17]. The standard PEP methodology is now a mature technology for worst-case analysis, supported by software packages such as PEPit [GMG+24].

However, standard PEP formulations analyze a fixed number of iterations, with the number of variables and constraints typically growing quadratically with this horizon. Deriving closed-form guarantees valid for all iterations can also be challenging. Auto­mated Lyapunov anal­y­ses provide a complementary approach: restricting the search to prescribed families of Lyapunov anal­y­ses can give smaller SDPs whose number of variables and constraints is independent of the iteration horizon, or grows only linearly with it, facilitating concise, closed-form con­ver­gence proofs [TVSL18, TB19, UBTG25, UDGT+26]. A closely related framework uses integral quadratic constraints (IQCs), developed in robust control [MR97], to obtain con­ver­gence guarantees through linear matrix inequalities (LMIs) that can be checked by semi­definite programming [LRP16, MSE21]. Although searching over prescribed families of Lyapunov functions may give conservative bounds, these bounds can still match the actual worst-case behavior in many settings.

In this post, we derive the corresponding SDPs explicitly for two examples: an inexact gradient method, for which the Lyapunov function is fixed in advance, and a gradient method with memory, for which we search for a Lyapunov function within a prescribed family. The aim is to explain the main ideas in a simple setting and provide a starting point for anal­y­ses of other meth­ods and problem classes. For the first example, we also show how to extract a closed-form proof of a tight con­ver­gence guarantee from numerical SDP solutions. In the second example, we show how allowing a more flexible class of Lyapunov functions can give tighter con­ver­gence guarantees. This post assumes familiarity with smooth and strongly convex op­ti­mi­za­tion, basic matrix algebra, and Lagrangian duality. On a first reading, the expandable derivations and proofs can be skipped.

1. Problem setting

For simplicity, both examples use the familiar setting of smooth and strongly convex op­ti­mi­za­tion, although the tools developed here apply more broadly. We consider the unconstrained problem

minimize𝑥∈ℝ𝑑𝑓(𝑥)(1)(1)minimizex∈Rdf(x)\begin{equation} \label{eq:optimization-problem} \mathop{\text{minimize}}\limits_{x \in \mathbb{R}^d}\; f(x) \end{equation}

where 𝑓:ℝ𝑑→ℝf:Rd→Rf:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R} is differentiable, has an 𝐿LL-Lipschitz continuous gradient (that is, 𝑓ff is 𝐿LL-smooth), and is 𝜇μ\mu-strongly convex, with 0<𝜇<𝐿0<μ<L0<\mu<L. We denote this class of functions by F𝜇,𝐿(ℝ𝑑)Fμ,L(Rd)\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^d). Equivalently, 𝑓ff satisfies

(∀𝑥,𝑦∈ℝ𝑑)[𝑓(𝑥)⩽𝑓(𝑦)+⟨∇𝑓(𝑦),𝑥−𝑦⟩+𝐿2‖𝑥−𝑦‖2,𝑓(𝑥)⩾𝑓(𝑦)+⟨∇𝑓(𝑦),𝑥−𝑦⟩+𝜇2‖𝑥−𝑦‖2,(2)(2)(∀x,y∈Rd)[f(x)⩽f(y)+⟨∇f(y),x−y⟩+L2‖x−y‖2,f(x)⩾f(y)+⟨∇f(y),x−y⟩+μ2‖x−y‖2,\begin{equation} \label{eq:quadratic-bounds} (\forall x,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d})\qquad \left[ \begin{aligned} f(x) &\leqslant f(y)+\langle\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle +\tfrac{L}{2}\lVert x-y\rVert^{2},\\ f(x) &\geqslant f(y)+\langle\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle +\tfrac{\mu}{2}\lVert x-y\rVert^{2}, \end{aligned} \right. \end{equation}

where ⟨⋅,⋅⟩⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle is the Euclidean inner product and ‖⋅‖‖⋅‖\lVert\cdot\rVert is its induced norm. For the quadratic bounds above, see [Bec17, Theorems 5.8(ii) and 5.24(ii)]. Strong convexity ensures that problem (1)(1)\eqref{eq:optimization-problem} has a unique minimizer 𝑥⋆∈ℝ𝑑x⋆∈Rdx^\star\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, characterized by ∇𝑓(𝑥⋆)=0∇f(x⋆)=0\nabla f(x^\star)=0 [Bec17, Theorems 3.63 and 5.25(a)]. Figure 1 illustrates these inequalities geometrically, showing how 𝑓ff is globally bounded above and below by quadratic functions tangent to it at any chosen point.

2. Fixed Lyapunov functions

Here we check a Lyapunov function chosen in advance, then use the tools developed here to search for one in Section 3.

2.1 The gradient method with inexact gradients

The standard gradient method provides a familiar starting point; here, we consider a slightly richer variant with inexact gradients. Given a constant step size 𝛾>0γ>0\gamma>0 and an initial point 𝑥0∈ℝ𝑑x0∈Rdx^{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, consider

[Pick 𝑑𝑘∈ℝ𝑑such that‖∇𝑓(𝑥𝑘)−𝑑𝑘‖⩽𝜀‖∇𝑓(𝑥𝑘)‖,𝑥𝑘+1=𝑥𝑘−𝛾𝑑𝑘,(3)(3)[Pick dk∈Rdsuch that‖∇f(xk)−dk‖⩽ε‖∇f(xk)‖,xk+1=xk−γdk,\begin{equation} \label{eq:relatively-inexact-gradient-method} \left[ \begin{aligned} &\text{Pick }d^{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\;\text{such that}\; \|\nabla f(x^{k}) - d^{k}\| \leqslant \varepsilon \|\nabla f(x^{k})\|,\\ &x^{k+1} = x^{k} - \gamma d^{k}, \end{aligned} \right. \end{equation}

where 𝜀∈[0,1)ε∈[0,1)\varepsilon\in[0,1) bounds the relative error in the gradient approximation. We seek convergence guarantees that hold for every sequence of approximations 𝑑𝑘dkd^k satisfying this bound. When 𝜀=0ε=0\varepsilon=0, we recover the standard gradient method.

We call such a quantity a performance measure. Under the standing assumptions, it is natural to seek bounds of the form

0⩽𝜌𝚗𝚘𝚛𝚖2(𝛾,𝜀,𝜇,𝐿)<1and0⩽𝜌𝚏𝚞𝚗𝚌(𝛾,𝜀,𝜇,𝐿)<1.0⩽ρnorm2(γ,ε,μ,L)<1and0⩽ρfunc(γ,ε,μ,L)<1.\begin{equation*} 0\leqslant \rho_{\mathtt{norm}^2}(\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L) < 1 \quad\text{and}\quad 0\leqslant \rho_{\mathtt{func}}(\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L) < 1. \end{equation*}

2.3 Optimal contraction via semidefinite programming

To verify (5)(5)\eqref{eq:lyapunov-contraction} along every trajectory, it suffices to consider one step from an arbitrary point 𝑥𝑘xkx^{k}. The update rule and the coefficients 𝑄QQ and 𝑞qq are the same at every iteration, and any such step can be realized as the first step by setting 𝑥0=𝑥𝑘x0=xkx^{0}=x^{k}. We therefore define the optimal one-step contraction factor by

𝜌⋆𝑑(𝑄,𝑞,𝛾,𝜀,𝜇,𝐿)=inf⎧{ {⎨{ {⎩𝜌∈ℝ∣ ∣ ∣ ∣V(𝑘+1)⩽𝜌V(𝑘)for every 𝑓∈F𝜇,𝐿(ℝ𝑑)and𝑥𝑘,𝑑𝑘∈ℝ𝑑 with𝑥𝑘+1=𝑥𝑘−𝛾𝑑𝑘and‖∇𝑓(𝑥𝑘)−𝑑𝑘‖⩽𝜀‖∇𝑓(𝑥𝑘)‖⎫{ {⎬{ {⎭.ρd⋆(Q,q,γ,ε,μ,L)=inf{ρ∈R|V(k+1)⩽ρV(k)for every f∈Fμ,L(Rd)andxk,dk∈Rd withxk+1=xk−γdkand‖∇f(xk)−dk‖⩽ε‖∇f(xk)‖}.\begin{equation*} \rho_d^{\star}(Q,q,\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L) =\inf\left\{ \rho\in\mathbb{R}\;\middle|\; \begin{array}{l} \mathcal{V}(k+1)\leqslant\rho\mathcal{V}(k)\\ \text{for every }f\in\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) \;\text{and}\; x^{k},d^{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\text{ with}\\ x^{k+1}=x^{k}-\gamma d^{k}\quad\text{and}\quad \|\nabla f(x^{k})-d^{k}\|\leqslant\varepsilon\|\nabla f(x^{k})\| \end{array} \right\}. \end{equation*}

We will show, step by step, how semidefinite programming gives an upper bound on this quantity and under which conditions the bound equals the optimal one-step contraction factor. We first fix a candidate 𝜌ρ\rho and derive a semidefinite feasibility test, then minimize 𝜌ρ\rho in this test. This feasibility formulation will also let us search for valid Lyapunov functions in Section 3, where their coefficients become additional variables.

Worst-case Lyapunov difference. For a fixed candidate 𝜌ρ\rho, we maximize the difference V(𝑘+1)−𝜌V(𝑘)V(k+1)−ρV(k)\mathcal{V}(k+1)-\rho\mathcal{V}(k) over all admissible functions and updates:

P𝑑(𝑄,𝑞,𝛾,𝜀,𝜇,𝐿,𝜌)=⎛⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜⎝maximize𝑓∈F𝜇,𝐿(ℝ𝑑)𝑥𝑘,𝑥𝑘+1,𝑥⋆,𝑑𝑘∈ℝ𝑑V(𝑘+1)−𝜌V(𝑘)subject to𝑥𝑘+1=𝑥𝑘−𝛾𝑑𝑘,‖∇𝑓(𝑥𝑘)−𝑑𝑘‖⩽𝜀‖∇𝑓(𝑥𝑘)‖,∇𝑓(𝑥⋆)=0⎞⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟⎠.Pd(Q,q,γ,ε,μ,L,ρ)=(maximizef∈Fμ,L(Rd)xk,xk+1,x⋆,dk∈RdV(k+1)−ρV(k)subject toxk+1=xk−γdk,‖∇f(xk)−dk‖⩽ε‖∇f(xk)‖,∇f(x⋆)=0).\begin{equation*} \mathcal{P}_{d}(Q,q,\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L,\rho) = \left( \begin{array}{cl} \mathop{\text{maximize}}\limits_{\substack{ f\in\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\\ x^{k},x^{k+1},x^{\star},d^{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} }} & \mathcal{V}(k+1)-\rho\,\mathcal{V}(k)\\[0.3em] \text{subject to} & x^{k+1}=x^{k}-\gamma d^{k},\\ & \norm{\nabla f(x^{k})-d^{k}}\leqslant\varepsilon\norm{\nabla f(x^{k})},\\ & \nabla f(x^{\star})=0 \end{array} \right). \end{equation*}

The contraction inequality (5)(5)\eqref{eq:lyapunov-contraction} holds for every admissible function and update exactly when P𝑑(𝑄,𝑞,𝛾,𝜀,𝜇,𝐿,𝜌)⩽0Pd(Q,q,γ,ε,μ,L,ρ)⩽0\mathcal{P}_{d}(Q,q,\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L,\rho)\leqslant0. The optimal one-step contraction factor is therefore

𝜌⋆𝑑(𝑄,𝑞,𝛾,𝜀,𝜇,𝐿)=inf{𝜌∈ℝ∣P𝑑(𝑄,𝑞,𝛾,𝜀,𝜇,𝐿,𝜌)⩽0}.ρd⋆(Q,q,γ,ε,μ,L)=inf{ρ∈R∣Pd(Q,q,γ,ε,μ,L,ρ)⩽0}.\begin{equation*} \rho_d^{\star}(Q,q,\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L) =\inf\{\rho\in\mathbb{R}\mid\mathcal{P}_{d}(Q,q,\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L,\rho)\leqslant0\}. \end{equation*}

We next derive a semidefinite test for the condition P𝑑(𝑄,𝑞,𝛾,𝜀,𝜇,𝐿,𝜌)⩽0Pd(Q,q,γ,ε,μ,L,ρ)⩽0\mathcal{P}_{d}(Q,q,\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L,\rho)\leqslant0. We will describe the possible function values and gradients using finitely many inequalities, collect vector inner products in a positive semidefinite matrix, and combine these inequalities to certify contraction.

Encoding inner products with a Gram matrix. Before we proceed, we introduce some convenient notation. Let 𝕊𝑛Sn\mathbb{S}^{n} and 𝕊𝑛+S+n\mathbb{S}_{+}^{n} denote the sets of real-valued symmetric and positive semidefinite 𝑛×𝑛n×nn\times n matrices, respectively. We define the Gramian function 𝙶𝚛𝚊𝚖:(ℝ𝑑)𝑛→𝕊𝑛+Gram:(Rd)n→S+n\mathtt{Gram}:(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n}\to\mathbb{S}^{n}_{+} by

(∀𝐳=(𝑧1,…,𝑧𝑛)∈(ℝ𝑑)𝑛)𝙶𝚛𝚊𝚖(𝐳)=(⟨𝑧𝑖,𝑧𝑗⟩)1⩽𝑖,𝑗⩽𝑛.(∀z=(z1,…,zn)∈(Rd)n)Gram(z)=(⟨zi,zj⟩)1⩽i,j⩽n.\begin{align*} (\forall \mathbf{z}=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n})\in(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n}) \qquad \mathtt{Gram}(\mathbf{z}) = (\inner{z_i}{z_j})_{1\leqslant i,j \leqslant n}. \end{align*}

V(𝑘)=trace(𝑄𝙶𝚛𝚊𝚖(𝑥𝑘−𝑥⋆,∇𝑓(𝑥𝑘)))+𝑞(𝑓(𝑥𝑘)−𝑓(𝑥⋆)).V(k)=trace(QGram(xk−x⋆,∇f(xk)))+q(f(xk)−f(x⋆)).\begin{align*} \mathcal{V}(k) = \text{trace}(Q\,\mathtt{Gram}(x^{k}-x^{\star} , \nabla f(x^{k}))) + q(f(x^{k})-f(x^{\star})). \end{align*}

For 𝐴∈ℝ𝑚×𝑛A∈Rm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, 𝑀∈𝕊𝑚M∈SmM\in\mathbb{S}^{m}, and 𝐳∈(ℝ𝑑)𝑛z∈(Rd)n\mathbf{z}\in(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n}, we will use the identities

Here, 𝑓ff is an infinite-dimensional optimization variable, even though only its values and gradients at 𝑥𝑘xkx^{k}, 𝑥𝑘+1xk+1x^{k+1}, and 𝑥⋆x⋆x^{\star} appear in the objective and constraints. Introducing corresponding variables 𝑓𝑖fif^i and 𝑔𝑖gig^i therefore gives the equivalent formulation

maximize𝑥𝑘,𝑥𝑘+1,𝑥⋆,𝑑𝑘∈ℝ𝑑𝑔𝑘,𝑔𝑘+1,𝑔⋆∈ℝ𝑑𝑓𝑘,𝑓𝑘+1,𝑓⋆∈ℝtrace((𝑆⊤+𝑄𝑆+−𝜌𝑆⊤𝑄𝑆)𝙶𝚛𝚊𝚖(𝑥𝑘−𝑥⋆,𝑔𝑘,𝑔𝑘+1,𝑑𝑘))+𝑞[−𝜌−1]⊤[𝑓𝑘−𝑓⋆𝑓𝑘+1−𝑓⋆]subject to𝑥𝑘+1=𝑥𝑘−𝛾𝑑𝑘,‖𝑔𝑘−𝑑𝑘‖⩽𝜀‖𝑔𝑘‖,𝑔⋆=0,there exists 𝑓∈F𝜇,𝐿(ℝ𝑑)such that𝑓(𝑥𝑖)=𝑓𝑖and∇𝑓(𝑥𝑖)=𝑔𝑖for each𝑖∈{𝑘,𝑘+1,⋆}.maximizexk,xk+1,x⋆,dk∈Rdgk,gk+1,g⋆∈Rdfk,fk+1,f⋆∈Rtrace((S+⊤QS+−ρS⊤QS)Gram(xk−x⋆,gk,gk+1,dk))+q[−ρ−1]⊤[fk−f⋆fk+1−f⋆]subject toxk+1=xk−γdk,‖gk−dk‖⩽ε‖gk‖,g⋆=0,there exists f∈Fμ,L(Rd)such thatf(xi)=fiand∇f(xi)=gifor eachi∈{k,k+1,⋆}.\begin{equation*} \begin{array}{cl} \mathop{\text{maximize}}\limits_{\substack{ x^{k},x^{k+1},x^{\star},d^{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\\ g^{k},g^{k+1},g^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\\ f^{k},f^{k+1},f^{\star}\in\mathbb{R} }} &\text{trace}((S_+^{\top}QS_+-\rho S^{\top}QS)\,\mathtt{Gram}(x^{k}-x^{\star},g^{k},g^{k+1},d^{k})) +q\begin{bmatrix}-\rho\\\phantom{-}1\end{bmatrix}^{\top} \begin{bmatrix} f^{k}-f^{\star}\\ f^{k+1}-f^{\star} \end{bmatrix} \\[0.6em] \text{subject to} &x^{k+1}=x^{k}-\gamma d^{k},\\ &\lVert g^{k}-d^{k}\rVert\leqslant\varepsilon\lVert g^{k}\rVert,\\ &g^{\star}=0,\\ &\text{there exists }f\in\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) \;\text{such that}\; f(x^i)=f^i\;\text{and}\; \nabla f(x^i)=g^i \;\text{for each}\; i\in\{k,k+1,\star\}. \end{array} \end{equation*}

At first glance, this may not seem like progress: we have replaced the infinite-dimensional variable by an existence constraint over the same function class. Have we actually made the problem any easier?

Determining whether the prescribed values and gradients can come from a single function in F𝜇,𝐿(ℝ𝑑)Fμ,L(Rd)\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is an interpolation problem. For this class, interpolation conditions from the performance estimation literature let us replace the existence constraint by finitely many explicit inequalities [THG17]. The quadratic bounds (2)(2)\eqref{eq:quadratic-bounds}, imposed only at the sampled points, are necessary but not sufficient for interpolation. Theorem 1 gives necessary and sufficient conditions for a function in F𝜇,𝐿(ℝ𝑑)Fμ,L(Rd)\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) to match all the prescribed values and gradients.

Theorem 1 (Smooth and strongly convex interpolation). [THG17, Theorem 4]

Let 𝐽JJ be a finite index set, and let 𝑥𝑖,𝑔𝑖∈ℝ𝑑xi,gi∈Rdx^i,g^i\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and 𝑓𝑖∈ℝfi∈Rf^i\in\mathbb{R} for each 𝑖∈𝐽i∈Ji\in J. There exists a function 𝑓∈F𝜇,𝐿(ℝ𝑑)f∈Fμ,L(Rd)f\in\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) satisfying

𝑓(𝑥𝑖)=𝑓𝑖and∇𝑓(𝑥𝑖)=𝑔𝑖for each𝑖∈𝐽f(xi)=fiand∇f(xi)=gifor eachi∈J\begin{equation*} f(x^i)=f^i\;\text{and}\; \nabla f(x^i)=g^i\;\text{for each}\; i\in J \end{equation*}

if and only if

𝑓𝑖−𝑓𝑗−⟨𝑔𝑗,𝑥𝑖−𝑥𝑗⟩⩾𝜇2‖𝑥𝑖−𝑥𝑗‖2+12(𝐿−𝜇)‖𝑔𝑖−𝑔𝑗−𝜇(𝑥𝑖−𝑥𝑗)‖2fi−fj−⟨gj,xi−xj⟩⩾μ2‖xi−xj‖2+12(L−μ)‖gi−gj−μ(xi−xj)‖2\begin{equation*} f^i-f^j-\inner{g^j}{x^i-x^j} \geqslant\tfrac{\mu}{2}\norm{x^i-x^j}^{2} +\tfrac{1}{2(L-\mu)}\norm{g^i-g^j-\mu(x^i-x^j)}^{2} \end{equation*}

for each pair of distinct indices 𝑖,𝑗∈𝐽i,j∈Ji,j\in J.

For an intuitive explanation of interpolation in the convex, possibly nonsmooth case, corresponding to 𝜇=0μ=0\mu=0 and 𝐿=+∞L=+∞L=+\infty, see Adrien Taylor’s excellent post on Francis Bach’s blog [Tay20].

Applying Theorem 1 gives the following equivalent finite-dimensional formulation, where we have squared the relative-error bound and written each inequality with zero on the right

maximize𝑥𝑘,𝑥𝑘+1,𝑥⋆,𝑑𝑘∈ℝ𝑑𝑔𝑘,𝑔𝑘+1,𝑔⋆∈ℝ𝑑𝑓𝑘,𝑓𝑘+1,𝑓⋆∈ℝtrace((𝑆⊤+𝑄𝑆+−𝜌𝑆⊤𝑄𝑆)𝙶𝚛𝚊𝚖(𝑥𝑘−𝑥⋆,𝑔𝑘,𝑔𝑘+1,𝑑𝑘))+𝑞[−𝜌−1]⊤[𝑓𝑘−𝑓⋆𝑓𝑘+1−𝑓⋆]subject to𝑥𝑘+1=𝑥𝑘−𝛾𝑑𝑘,‖𝑔𝑘−𝑑𝑘‖2−𝜀2‖𝑔𝑘‖2⩽0,𝑔⋆=0,𝑓𝑗−𝑓𝑖+⟨𝑔𝑗,𝑥𝑖−𝑥𝑗⟩+𝜇2‖𝑥𝑖−𝑥𝑗‖2+12(𝐿−𝜇)‖𝑔𝑖−𝑔𝑗−𝜇(𝑥𝑖−𝑥𝑗)‖2⩽0for each pair of distinct indices 𝑖,𝑗∈{𝑘,𝑘+1,⋆}.maximizexk,xk+1,x⋆,dk∈Rdgk,gk+1,g⋆∈Rdfk,fk+1,f⋆∈Rtrace((S+⊤QS+−ρS⊤QS)Gram(xk−x⋆,gk,gk+1,dk))+q[−ρ−1]⊤[fk−f⋆fk+1−f⋆]subject toxk+1=xk−γdk,‖gk−dk‖2−ε2‖gk‖2⩽0,g⋆=0,fj−fi+⟨gj,xi−xj⟩+μ2‖xi−xj‖2+12(L−μ)‖gi−gj−μ(xi−xj)‖2⩽0for each pair of distinct indices i,j∈{k,k+1,⋆}.\begin{equation*} \begin{array}{cl} \mathop{\text{maximize}}\limits_{\substack{ x^{k},x^{k+1},x^{\star},d^{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\\ g^{k},g^{k+1},g^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\\ f^{k},f^{k+1},f^{\star}\in\mathbb{R} }} &\text{trace}((S_+^{\top}QS_+-\rho S^{\top}QS)\,\mathtt{Gram}(x^{k}-x^{\star},g^{k},g^{k+1},d^{k})) +q\begin{bmatrix}-\rho\\\phantom{-}1\end{bmatrix}^{\top} \begin{bmatrix} f^{k}-f^{\star}\\ f^{k+1}-f^{\star} \end{bmatrix} \\[0.6em] \text{subject to} &x^{k+1}=x^{k}-\gamma d^{k},\\ &\norm{g^{k}-d^{k}}^{2}-\varepsilon^{2}\norm{g^{k}}^{2}\leqslant0,\\ &g^{\star}=0,\\ &f^j-f^i+\inner{g^j}{x^i-x^j} +\tfrac{\mu}{2}\norm{x^i-x^j}^{2} +\tfrac{1}{2(L-\mu)}\norm{g^i-g^j-\mu(x^i-x^j)}^{2}\leqslant0\\ &\text{for each pair of distinct indices }i,j\in\{k,k+1,\star\}. \end{array} \end{equation*}

We have now eliminated the unknown function: only finitely many vector and scalar variables remain. For the three indices in {𝑘,𝑘+1,⋆}{k,k+1,⋆}\{k,k+1,\star\}, there are six interpolation inequalities: one for each ordered pair of distinct indices. Swapping 𝑖ii and 𝑗jj generally gives a different inequality.

Rewriting the constraints. Substituting 𝑥𝑘+1=𝑥𝑘−𝛾𝑑𝑘xk+1=xk−γdkx^{k+1}=x^{k}-\gamma d^{k} and 𝑔⋆=0g⋆=0g^{\star}=0 eliminates 𝑥𝑘+1xk+1x^{k+1} and 𝑔⋆g⋆g^{\star} as optimization variables. The relative-error constraint becomes

for each pair of distinct indices 𝑖,𝑗∈{𝑘,𝑘+1,⋆}i,j∈{k,k+1,⋆}i,j\in\{k,k+1,\star\}.

The following result lets us replace the vectors by their Gram matrix, with a rank constraint accounting for the dimension 𝑑dd.

Which matrices are Gram matrices? For 𝐺∈𝕊𝑛G∈SnG\in\mathbb{S}^{n}, we have that

there exists 𝐳∈(ℝ𝑑)𝑛such that𝙶𝚛𝚊𝚖(𝐳)=𝐺if and only if𝐺∈𝕊𝑛+andrank⁡(𝐺)⩽𝑑.(8)(8)there exists z∈(Rd)nsuch thatGram(z)=Gif and only ifG∈S+nandrank⁡(G)⩽d.\begin{equation} \label{eq:gram-characterization} \text{there exists }\mathbf{z}\in(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n}\;\text{such that}\; \mathtt{Gram}(\mathbf{z})=G \;\text{if and only if}\; G\in\mathbb{S}_{+}^{n}\;\text{and}\;\mathord{\mathop{\text{rank}}\nolimits(G)}\leqslant d. \end{equation}

Here, solving the dual SDP amounts to finding multipliers satisfying its constraints. The primal relaxation and weak duality (the primal SDP optimal value is no larger than the dual SDP optimal value) [BV04, Section 5.2.2] give

P𝑑(𝑄,𝑞,𝛾,𝜀,𝜇,𝐿,𝜌)⩽PSDP(𝑄,𝑞,𝛾,𝜀,𝜇,𝐿,𝜌)⩽DSDP(𝑄,𝑞,𝛾,𝜀,𝜇,𝐿,𝜌).Pd(Q,q,γ,ε,μ,L,ρ)⩽PSDP(Q,q,γ,ε,μ,L,ρ)⩽DSDP(Q,q,γ,ε,μ,L,ρ).\begin{equation*} \mathcal{P}_{d}(Q,q,\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L,\rho) \leqslant\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{SDP}}(Q,q,\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L,\rho) \leqslant\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{SDP}}(Q,q,\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L,\rho). \end{equation*}

Thus, if we find such multipliers, the right-hand side is zero and P𝑑(𝑄,𝑞,𝛾,𝜀,𝜇,𝐿,𝜌)⩽0Pd(Q,q,γ,ε,μ,L,ρ)⩽0\mathcal{P}_{d}(Q,q,\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L,\rho)\leqslant0.

This follows from the refined Slater condition [BV04, Section 5.2.3]. The verification is technical, so we include it below as optional reading for those interested in the details.

At the sampled parameter values, the numerical results suggest that function-value suboptimality gives a one-step contraction factor no larger than that for the squared distance to the solution. Gannot [Gan22, Remark 1.6] states 𝑓(𝑥𝑘+1)−𝑓(𝑥⋆)⩽𝜌𝚏𝚞𝚗𝚌(𝛾,𝜀,𝜇,𝐿)(𝑓(𝑥𝑘)−𝑓(𝑥⋆))f(xk+1)−f(x⋆)⩽ρfunc(γ,ε,μ,L)(f(xk)−f(x⋆))f(x^{k+1})-f(x^\star)\leqslant\rho_{\mathtt{func}}(\gamma,\varepsilon,\mu,L)(f(x^k)-f(x^\star)), drawing on a proof by Etienne de Klerk, François Glineur, and Adrien B. Taylor [dKGT20, Appendix B]. A proof for 𝛾∈(0,𝛾⋆]γ∈(0,γ⋆]\gamma\in(0,\gamma_\star] is given by Uschmajew and Vandereycken [UV22, Theorem 4.2].

2.6 Optional: Reducing the certificate to two squared norms

We can simplify the sum of squares in (12)(12)\eqref{eq:function-value-sos-bound} by using weaker interpolation inequalities, while keeping the same contraction factor. 3. Searching for Lyapunov functions

In Section 2, we compared the one-step contraction factors obtained from squared distance to the solution and function-value suboptimality. A contracting Lyapunov function that bounds a performance measure from above can certify a faster asymptotic rate than a direct contraction bound for that measure, or establish convergence even when the measure does not contract at every iteration. Here we search for such a Lyapunov function within a chosen family. We illustrate this search using stationary gradient methods with memory to solve (1)(1)\eqref{eq:optimization-problem}, i.e., to minimize a function 𝑓∈F𝜇,𝐿(ℝ𝑑)f∈Fμ,L(Rd)f\in\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^d).

3.1 Stationary gradient methods with memory

Given constants 𝛾>0γ>0\gamma>0 and 𝛼,𝛽∈ℝα,β∈R\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}, and initial points 𝑥0,𝑥−1∈ℝ𝑑x0,x−1∈Rdx^{0},x^{-1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, consider

[𝑦𝑘=𝑥𝑘+𝛼(𝑥𝑘−𝑥𝑘−1),𝑥𝑘+1=𝑥𝑘−𝛾∇𝑓(𝑦𝑘)+𝛽(𝑥𝑘−𝑥𝑘−1).(14)(14)[yk=xk+α(xk−xk−1),xk+1=xk−γ∇f(yk)+β(xk−xk−1).\begin{equation} \label{eq:gradient-method-with-memory} \left[ \begin{aligned} y^{k} &= x^{k}+\alpha(x^{k}-x^{k-1}),\\ x^{k+1} &= x^{k}-\gamma\nabla f(y^{k})+\beta(x^{k}-x^{k-1}). \end{aligned} \right. \end{equation}

The method is called stationary because 𝛾γ\gamma, 𝛼α\alpha, and 𝛽β\beta are constant across iterations. In the table below, we give some standard choices of 𝛾γ\gamma, 𝛼α\alpha, and 𝛽β\beta.

  1. Gradient method: Optimal constant step size for worst-case distance contraction on F𝜇,𝐿(ℝ𝑑)Fμ,L(Rd)\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) [Pol63, Theorem 6; Nes18, Theorem 2.1.15].
  2. Polyak's heavy-ball method: Optimal parameters for worst-case asymptotic convergence on quadratics in F𝜇,𝐿(ℝ𝑑)Fμ,L(Rd)\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) [Pol64, Theorem 9(3) and the note on p. 15].
  3. Nesterov's method: Optimal dimension-independent decay exponent for convergence in distance on F𝜇,𝐿(ℝ𝑑)Fμ,L(Rd)\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), up to constant factors [Nes18, Theorem 2.2.1 and Equation (2.2.22); DT22, Corollary 3].
  4. Triple momentum method [VSFL18, Definition 2]: Optimal dimension-independent decay exponent for convergence in distance on F𝜇,𝐿(ℝ𝑑)Fμ,L(Rd)\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) [DT22, Corollary 3].
3.2 Choosing a family of Lyapunov functions

To establish a convergence rate for a nonnegative performance measure MM\mathcal{M}, we look for a Lyapunov function VV\mathcal{V} and a contraction factor 𝜌∈[0,1)ρ∈[0,1)\rho\in[0,1) satisfying

V(𝑘+1)⩽𝜌V(𝑘),V(𝑘)⩾M(𝑘)⩾0,(C1)(C2)(C1)V(k+1)⩽ρV(k),(C2)V(k)⩾M(k)⩾0,\begin{align} \mathcal{V}(k+1)&\leqslant\rho\mathcal{V}(k), \tag{C1}\label{eq:memory-lyapunov-contraction}\\ \mathcal{V}(k)&\geqslant\mathcal{M}(k)\geqslant0, \tag{C2}\label{eq:memory-lyapunov-lower-bound} \end{align}

for every 𝑘⩾0k⩾0k\geqslant0, every 𝑓∈F𝜇,𝐿(ℝ𝑑)f∈Fμ,L(Rd)f\in\mathcal{F}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb{R}^d), and every trajectory of (14)(14)\eqref{eq:gradient-method-with-memory}.

Condition (C1)(C1)\eqref{eq:memory-lyapunov-contraction} requires the Lyapunov function to contract, but imposing it alone would allow the trivial choice V≡0V≡0\mathcal{V}\equiv0, regardless of MM\mathcal{M}. Condition (C2)(C2)\eqref{eq:memory-lyapunov-lower-bound} connects the Lyapunov function to the performance measure by requiring VV\mathcal{V} to bound MM\mathcal{M} from above. Iterating (C1)(C1)\eqref{eq:memory-lyapunov-contraction} and applying (C2)(C2)\eqref{eq:memory-lyapunov-lower-bound} then gives, for 𝑘⩾0k⩾0k\geqslant0,

0⩽M(𝑘)⩽V(𝑘)⩽𝜌𝑘V(0)⟹M(𝑘)∈O(𝜌𝑘)as𝑘→∞.0⩽M(k)⩽V(k)⩽ρkV(0)⟹M(k)∈O(ρk)ask→∞.\begin{equation*} 0\leqslant\mathcal{M}(k)\leqslant\mathcal{V}(k)\leqslant\rho^k\mathcal{V}(0) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathcal{M}(k)\in\mathcal{O}(\rho^k) \quad\text{as}\quad k\to\infty. \end{equation*}

Thus, the performance measure MM\mathcal{M} converges linearly to zero with rate at most 𝜌ρ\rho. We can therefore keep the performance measure MM\mathcal{M} fixed and search for a contracting upper bound VV\mathcal{V}.

We restrict VV\mathcal{V} and MM\mathcal{M} to the following forms:

3.3 Optimal contraction via semidefinite programming

Adapting the argument of Section 2.3 separately to (C1)(C1)\eqref{eq:memory-lyapunov-contraction} and the inequality V(𝑘)⩾M(𝑘)V(k)⩾M(k)\mathcal{V}(k)\geqslant\mathcal{M}(k) in (C2)(C2)\eqref{eq:memory-lyapunov-lower-bound} gives Theorem 3. Nonnegativity of MM\mathcal{M} is ensured by our choice of 𝑃,𝑝P,pP,p. For completeness, we include a proof for the interested reader after the formal statement.

Theorem 3 (Semi­definite tests for the Lyapunov inequalities).

Primal formulation. The Gram characterization (8)(8)\eqref{eq:gram-characterization} and Theorem 1 give the following equivalent finite-dimensional formulation

PC1,𝑑=⎛⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜⎝maximize𝐺∈𝕊4+,𝐹∈ℝ2trace((𝑆⊤+𝑄𝑆+−𝜌𝑆⊤𝑄𝑆)𝐺)+𝑞[−𝜌−1]⊤𝐹subject torank⁡(𝐺)⩽𝑑,trace(𝐴C1𝑖,𝑗𝐺)+(𝑎C1𝑖,𝑗)⊤𝐹⩽0⎞⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟⎠.PC1,d=(maximizeG∈S+4,F∈R2trace((S+⊤QS+−ρS⊤QS)G)+q[−ρ−1]⊤Fsubject torank⁡(G)⩽d,trace(Ai,jC1G)+(ai,jC1)⊤F⩽0).\begin{equation*} \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{C1},d} =\left( \begin{array}{cl} \mathop{\text{maximize}}\limits_{G\in\mathbb{S}_{+}^{4},\,F\in\mathbb{R}^{2}} &\text{trace}((S_+^{\top}QS_+-\rho S^{\top}QS)G) +q\begin{bmatrix}-\rho\\\phantom{-}1\end{bmatrix}^{\top}F\\[0.6em] \text{subject to} &\mathop{\text{rank}}\nolimits(G)\leqslant d,\\ &\text{trace}(A_{i,j}^{\mathrm{C1}}G)+(a_{i,j}^{\mathrm{C1}})^{\top}F\leqslant0 \end{array} \right). \end{equation*}

Dropping the rank constraint gives the primal SDP

PSDPC1=⎛⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜⎝maximize𝐺∈𝕊4+,𝐹∈ℝ2trace((𝑆⊤+𝑄𝑆+−𝜌𝑆⊤𝑄𝑆)𝐺)+𝑞[−𝜌−1]⊤𝐹subject totrace(𝐴C1𝑖,𝑗𝐺)+(𝑎C1𝑖,𝑗)⊤𝐹⩽0⎞⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟⎠,PC1SDP=(maximizeG∈S+4,F∈R2trace((S+⊤QS+−ρS⊤QS)G)+q[−ρ−1]⊤Fsubject totrace(Ai,jC1G)+(ai,jC1)⊤F⩽0),\begin{equation*} \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{C1}}^{\mathrm{SDP}} =\left( \begin{array}{cl} \mathop{\text{maximize}}\limits_{G\in\mathbb{S}_{+}^{4},\,F\in\mathbb{R}^{2}} &\text{trace}((S_+^{\top}QS_+-\rho S^{\top}QS)G) +q\begin{bmatrix}-\rho\\\phantom{-}1\end{bmatrix}^{\top}F\\[0.6em] \text{subject to} &\text{trace}(A_{i,j}^{\mathrm{C1}}G)+(a_{i,j}^{\mathrm{C1}})^{\top}F\leqslant0 \end{array} \right), \end{equation*}

and hence

PC1,𝑑⩽PSDPC1.PC1,d⩽PC1SDP.\begin{equation*} \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{C1},d}\leqslant\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{C1}}^{\mathrm{SDP}}. \end{equation*}

For 𝑑⩾4d⩾4d\geqslant4, the rank constraint is automatic, so

PC1,𝑑=PSDPC1.PC1,d=PC1SDP.\begin{equation*} \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{C1},d}=\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{C1}}^{\mathrm{SDP}}. \end{equation*}

for each pair of distinct indices 𝑖,𝑗∈{𝑘,𝑘+1,⋆}i,j∈{k,k+1,⋆}i,j\in\{k,k+1,\star\}. With the notation 𝜆C1=(𝜆C1𝑖,𝑗)𝑖,𝑗∈{𝑘,𝑘+1,⋆},𝑖≠𝑗λC1=(λi,jC1)i,j∈{k,k+1,⋆},i≠j\lambda^{\mathrm{C1}}=(\lambda_{i,j}^{\mathrm{C1}})_{i,j\in\{k,k+1,\star\},\,i\ne j}, the Lagrangian is

    𝑥𝑘=(1,0,0),𝑥𝑘−1=(0,1,1),|det𝑍|=ℓ3−ℓ2>0.xk=(1,0,0),xk−1=(0,1,1),|detZ|=ℓ3−ℓ2>0.\begin{equation*} \begin{gathered} x^k=(1,0,0),\qquad x^{k-1}=(0,1,1),\\[0.5em] |\det Z| =\ell_3-\ell_2>0. \end{gathered} \end{equation*}

Thus 𝐺=𝑍⊤𝑍≻0G=Z⊤Z≻0G=Z^{\top}Z\succ0 in both cases. The refined Slater condition therefore gives

PC2,𝑑=PSDPC2=DSDPC2=0.PC2,d=PC2SDP=DC2SDP=0.\begin{equation*} \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{C2},d}=\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{C2}}^{\mathrm{SDP}}=\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{C2}}^{\mathrm{SDP}}=0. \end{equation*}

In particular, the dual SDP is feasible, and its multipliers satisfy (18)(18)\eqref{eq:memory-lower-bound-certificate}.

Searching for a Lyapunov function. We now let the parameters 𝑄,𝑞Q,qQ,q defining VV\mathcal{V} vary and minimize 𝜌ρ\rho subject to both tests in Theorem 3. The resulting problem has bilinear terms 𝜌𝑄ρQ\rho Q and 𝜌𝑞ρq\rho q, but becomes an SDP feasibility problem when 𝜌ρ\rho is fixed. We denote its optimal value by

Two observations allow us to use bisection with an SDP solver:

  1. SDP feasibility. With 𝜌ρ\rho fixed, the constraints in (21)(21)\eqref{eq:memory-lyapunov-search} are affine in 𝑄,𝑞Q,qQ,q and the multipliers 𝜆C1,𝜆C2λC1,λC2\lambda^{\mathrm{C1}},\lambda^{\mathrm{C2}}, so we have an SDP feasibility problem.

  2. Monotonicity. If (21)(21)\eqref{eq:memory-lyapunov-search} is feasible at 𝜌ρ\rho, it is feasible at every 𝜌′∈(𝜌,1)ρ′∈(ρ,1)\rho'\in(\rho,1).

    Show proofHide proof

    A feasible point gives V(𝑘)⩾M(𝑘)⩾0V(k)⩾M(k)⩾0\mathcal{V}(k)\geqslant\mathcal{M}(k)\geqslant0. Hence

    V(𝑘+1)⩽𝜌V(𝑘)⩽𝜌′V(𝑘).V(k+1)⩽ρV(k)⩽ρ′V(k).\begin{equation*} \mathcal{V}(k+1)\leqslant\rho\mathcal{V}(k)\leqslant\rho'\mathcal{V}(k). \end{equation*}

    Since (21)(21)\eqref{eq:memory-lyapunov-search} does not depend on 𝑑dd, we can take 𝑑=4d=4d=4 and apply the necessity part of Theorem 3 to obtain C1 multipliers 𝜆C1λC1\lambda^{\mathrm{C1}} for 𝜌′ρ′\rho', with the same 𝑄,𝑞Q,qQ,q. Together with the original C2 multipliers 𝜆C2λC2\lambda^{\mathrm{C2}}, these give a feasible point of (21)(21)\eqref{eq:memory-lyapunov-search} at 𝜌′ρ′\rho'.

We can therefore use bisection to search for the smallest contraction factor 𝜌ρ\rho certifiable by (21)(21)\eqref{eq:memory-lyapunov-search}, which is also the smallest factor within the class of Lyapunov functions in (15)(15)\eqref{eq:memory-lyapunov-ansatz} when 𝑑⩾4d⩾4d\geqslant4.

3.4 Numerical results

The numerical results were obtained with MOSEK [Mos26].

For M(𝑘)=‖𝑥𝑘−𝑥⋆‖2M(k)=‖xk−x⋆‖2\mathcal{M}(k)=\|x^k-x^\star\|^2, we now use numerical bisection to estimate the optimal value of (21)(21)\eqref{eq:memory-lyapunov-search} for the four methods in Section 3.1, using the parameters given there. Figure 4 compares the results with and without the additional constraints 𝑄≽0Q≽0Q\succcurlyeq0 and 𝑞⩾0q⩾0q\geqslant0.

For the parameter choices in Section 3.1, the optimal value 𝜌⋆ρ⋆\rho^\star of (21)(21)\eqref{eq:memory-lyapunov-search} depends only on the ratio 𝐿/𝜇L/μL/\mu, which explains the horizontal axis in Figure 4 and allows us to compute the curves with 𝐿=1L=1L=1 and 𝜇∈(0,1)μ∈(0,1)\mu\in(0,1).

Thus the two meth­ods generate the same iterates from the same initial points.

̃𝑄=𝐷⊤𝑄𝐷,𝑄=𝐷−⊤̃𝑄𝐷−1,̃𝑞=𝐿𝑞,𝑞=1𝐿̃𝑞.Q~=D⊤QD,Q=D−⊤Q~D−1,q~=Lq,q=1Lq~.\begin{equation*} \begin{alignedat}{2} \widetilde Q&=D^{\top}QD,\qquad &Q&=D^{-\top}\widetilde QD^{-1},\\[0.4em] \widetilde q&=Lq, &q&=\tfrac{1}{L}\widetilde q. \end{alignedat} \end{equation*}

Hence (C1)(C1)\eqref{eq:memory-lyapunov-contraction} and (C2)(C2)\eqref{eq:memory-lyapunov-lower-bound} hold with the same 𝜌ρ\rho in either setting.

Since (21)(21)\eqref{eq:memory-lyapunov-search} does not depend on 𝑑dd, Theorem 3 at 𝑑=4d=4d=4 gives equivalent SDP feasibility before and after normalization. The optimal values therefore agree:

𝜌⋆(𝑃,0,𝛾,𝛼,𝛽,𝜇,𝐿)=𝜌⋆(𝑃,0,𝐿𝛾,𝛼,𝛽,𝜇𝐿,1).ρ⋆(P,0,γ,α,β,μ,L)=ρ⋆(P,0,Lγ,α,β,μL,1).\begin{equation*} \rho^\star(P,0,\gamma,\alpha,\beta,\mu,L) =\rho^\star(P,0,L\gamma,\alpha,\beta,\tfrac{\mu}{L},1). \end{equation*}

The right-hand side depends only on 𝜇/𝐿μ/L\mu/L for the parameter choices in Section 3.1. The same argument applies when the additional constraints are imposed, because

𝑄≽0⟺̃𝑄≽0,𝑞⩾0⟺̃𝑞⩾0.Q≽0⟺Q~≽0,q⩾0⟺q~⩾0.\begin{equation*} Q\succcurlyeq0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\widetilde Q\succcurlyeq0, \qquad q\geqslant0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\widetilde q\geqslant0. \end{equation*}

Conclusions. Removing the additional constraints 𝑄≽0Q≽0Q\succcurlyeq0 and 𝑞⩾0q⩾0q\geqslant0 can improve the certified contraction factors. For triple momentum at larger condition numbers, the search without these additional constraints still certifies contraction, while no factor below 111 is found when they are imposed. The restricted family includes familiar choices such as squared distance to the solution, function-value suboptimality, and squared gradient norm, illustrating the value of searching over a more flexible class of Lyapunov functions.

4. Going further

Both examples use semi­definite programming to combine valid inequalities into a Lyapunov certificate, either for a fixed Lyapunov function or while searching for one within a chosen family.

The theoretical framework in [UBTG25] extends these ideas beyond the contraction bounds considered here. It covers sublinear con­ver­gence guarantees and splitting meth­ods, including proximal gradient and Douglas–Rachford.

AutoLyap, described in [UDGT+26], supports broader classes of op­ti­mi­za­tion and in­clu­sion prob­lems, iteration-dependent meth­ods and anal­y­ses, and richer families of Lyapunov functions. Users specify the problem class, method, and desired Lyapunov analysis through a high-level interface. The software constructs and numerically solves the corresponding SDPs. Its documentation provides worked examples.

Acknowledgements and use of generative AI. I thank Adrien Taylor and Adrien Banse for their helpful comments and suggestions. Large language models (LLMs) were used to help produce figures, correct typos, and improve wording.
